paragraphs: Irish soldiers came home from Lebanon on Friday. They landed at Dublin Airport at about 2pm. Their families were waiting for them.
The soldiers were part of a United Nations peace mission. They spent six months in the south of Lebanon. It is a dangerous area.
This group was the last Irish battalion with the mission. There were about 344 soldiers. Sixteen of them were women. For 114 soldiers, it was their first trip abroad with the army.
Their leader, Lieutenant Colonel Damian Carroll, said it was the end of an era. A smaller Irish group will now go to Lebanon. The Irish camp there will close in December.
Many soldiers were very happy and emotional. One soldier from Cork was met by his young son.

paragraphs: Families and friends cheered loudly at Dublin Airport on Friday afternoon as Irish soldiers returned home from Lebanon. The soldiers had spent six months in the south of the country with UNIFIL, the United Nations peacekeeping mission there.

The group, called the 128th Infantry Battalion, is the last Irish battalion that will serve with the mission. Irish troops have worked in southern Lebanon since 1978, so many people see this as a very important moment.

About 344 people were in the battalion, including 16 women. They came from 28 counties, and Dublin had the largest number, with 43. For 114 of them, this was their first time working overseas with the Defence Forces.

The commanding officer, Lieutenant Colonel Damian Carroll, said it was the end of an era for the Defence Forces. He also called it the beginning of the end for the UN mission, which will start to close in 2027.

The soldiers arrived in May, soon after fighting started in southern Lebanon in March. Some peacekeepers from other countries were killed before they arrived. Later, the situation became calmer, and the soldiers helped people who had to leave their homes.
A smaller Irish unit will now replace the battalion, and Camp Shamrock, the main Irish base, will close in December. The battalion will bring all its equipment back to Ireland.
At the airport, there were many emotional moments. One soldier from Cork was met by his three-year-old son, and others said they were looking forward to spending time with their families.

paragraphs: There were emotional scenes at Dublin Airport on Friday afternoon as the last Irish battalion to serve with the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) returned home after a six-month deployment.

The 128th Infantry Battalion was greeted with loud applause when it arrived at around 2pm. Ireland has contributed troops to the peacekeeping mission in southern Lebanon since 1978, and the homecoming marks the end of a long chapter in the history of the Defence Forces.
The battalion had about 344 members, 16 of them women. Its personnel came from 28 counties, with Dublin providing the largest number at 43, and 114 soldiers were serving overseas for the first time.

Their commanding officer, Lieutenant Colonel Damian Carroll, described the return as the end of an era. He said it was also the beginning of the end for UNIFIL, which is preparing to withdraw from the region in 2027.

The troops deployed in May, shortly after hostilities broke out in southern Lebanon in March, and several international peacekeepers were killed just before they arrived. As tensions later eased, the mission returned to local duties, including support for displaced people.

The battalion is being replaced by a smaller infantry group, and Camp Shamrock, the Irish headquarters in the area, is due to close next month. All of the battalion's equipment will be brought back to Ireland.

For the families waiting in the arrivals hall, however, the main feeling was relief. A soldier from Cork was welcomed by his three-year-old son, while others spoke of looking forward to time with their partners and children.

paragraphs: Dublin Airport witnessed poignant scenes on Friday afternoon as the final Irish battalion to serve with the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) arrived home following a six-month tour of duty.

The 128th Infantry Battalion touched down at around 2pm to rapturous applause. Irish peacekeepers have been stationed in southern Lebanon since 1978, and their homecoming draws a line under one of the most enduring commitments in the history of the Defence Forces.

The contingent numbered roughly 344, including 16 women. Its ranks were drawn from 28 counties, with Dublin supplying the largest share at 43, while 114 personnel were embarking on their maiden overseas posting.

Lieutenant Colonel Damian Carroll, the commanding officer, characterised the occasion as the end of an era, adding that it heralded the beginning of the end for UNIFIL, which is slated to wind down its operations in 2027.

The troops were deployed in May, in the wake of hostilities that erupted in southern Lebanon in March and claimed the lives of several international peacekeepers shortly before their arrival. Once the volatile situation subsided, the mission reverted to local operations, notably assisting displaced civilians.
A pared-back infantry group is taking over from the battalion, and Camp Shamrock, the Irish base in the region, is set to close next month. The unit's entire stock of equipment is to be repatriated.

In the arrivals hall, though, geopolitics took a back seat to heartfelt reunions. One Cork soldier was embraced by his three-year-old son, while comrades spoke of savouring long-awaited time with loved ones.

第128步兵營約在下午兩點降落，迎來熱烈的掌聲。

這支分遣隊約有344人，其中包括16名女性。
成員來自28個郡，都柏林占比最大，有43人，另有114名人員是首次派駐海外。
指揮官達米安・卡羅爾中校形容此刻是一個時代的結束，並補充說這預示著UNIFIL走向終點的開始，該部隊預定於2027年逐步結束行動。
部隊於五月派駐，當時黎巴嫩南部在三月爆發敵對行動，並在他們抵達前不久奪走了數名國際維和人員的性命。
